entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5588"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 16</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11">Psa 16:1-11</reference>. Michtam, or, by the change of one letter, Michtab--a "writing," such as a poem or song (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.38.9">Is 38:9</reference>). Such a change of the letter m for b was not unusual. The position of this word in connection with the author's name, being that usually occupied by some term, such as Psalm or song, denoting the style or matter of the composition, favors this view of its meaning, though we know not why this and Psalms 56-60 should be specially, called "a writing." "A</title> <div sID="gen8490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">golden (Psalm)," or "a memorial" are explanations proposed by some--</hi>neither of which, however applicable here, appears adapted to the other Psalms where the term occurs. According to Peter (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.25">Ac 2:25</reference>) and Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.35">Ac 13:35</reference>), this Psalm relates to Christ and expresses the feelings of His human nature, in view of His sufferings and victory over death and the grave, including His subsequent exaltation at the right hand of God. Such was the exposition of the best earlier Christian interpreters. Some moderns have held that the Psalm relates exclusively to David; but this view is expressly contradicted by the apostles; others hold that the language of the Psalm is applicable to David as a type of Christ, capable of the higher sense assigned it in the New Testament. But then the language of <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference> cannot be used of David in any sense, for "he saw corruption." Others again propose to refer the first part to David, and the last to Christ; but it is evident that no change in the subject of the Psalm is indicated. Indeed, the person who appeals to God for help is evidently the same who rejoices in having found it. In referring the whole Psalm to Christ, it is, however, by no means denied that much of its language is expressive of the feelings of His people, so far as in their humble measure they have the feelings of trust in God expressed by Him, their head and representative. Such use of His language, as recorded in His last prayer (<reference osisRef="John.17.1-John.17.26">Joh 17:1-26</reference>), and even that which He used in Gethsemane, under similar modifications, is equally proper. The propriety of this reference of the Psalm to Christ will appear in the scope and interpretation. In view of the sufferings before Him, the Saviour, with that instinctive dread of death manifested in Gethsemane, calls on God to "preserve" Him; He avows His delight in holiness and abhorrence of the wicked and their wickedness; and for "the joy that was set before Him, despising the shame" [He 12:2], encourages Himself; contemplating the glories of the heritage appointed Him. Thus even death and the grave lose their terrors in the assurance of the victory to be attained and "the glory that should follow" [1Pe 1:11].<div eID="gen8490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8491" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5588"/><hi type="bold">1. I ... trust--</hi>as one seeking shelter from pressing danger. <div eID="gen8492" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5589"/><div sID="gen8493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5589"/><hi type="bold">2. my soul--</hi>must be supplied; expressed in similar cases (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.5">Psa 42:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen8493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my goodness ... thee--</hi>This obscure passage is variously expounded. Either one of two expositions falls in with the context. "My goodness" or merit is not on account of Thee--that is, is not for Thy benefit. Then follows the contrast of <reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Psa 16:3</reference> (but is), in respect, or for the saints, &c.--that is, it enures to them. Or, my goodness--or happiness is not besides Thee--that is, without Thee I have no other source of happiness. Then, "to the saints," &c., means that the same privilege of deriving happiness from God only is theirs. The first is the most consonant with the Messianic character of the Psalm, though the latter is not inconsistent with it. <div eID="gen8494" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5591"/><div sID="gen8498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5591"/>4. He expresses his abhorrence of those who seek other sources of happiness or objects of worship, and, by characterizing their rites by drink offerings of blood, clearly denotes idolaters. The word for "sorrows" is by some rendered "idols"; but, though a similar word to that for idols, it is not the same. In selecting such a term, there may be an allusion, by the author, to the sorrows produced by idolatrous practices. <div eID="gen8498" type="x-p"/>

This use of "soul" for the person is frequent (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.5">Ge 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.46.26">46:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.3.2">Psa 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.2">7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">11:1</reference>), even when the body may be the part chiefly affected, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.13">Psa 35:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.18">105:18</reference>. Some cases are cited, as <reference osisRef="Lev.22.4">Le 22:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.6.6">Nu 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.9.6">9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.9.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.19.13">19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hag.2.13">Hag 2:13</reference>, &c., which seem to justify assigning the meaning of body, or dead body; but it will be found that the latter sense is given by some adjunct expressed or implied. In those cases person is the proper sense.<div eID="gen8509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wilt not leave ... hell--</hi>abandon to the power of (<reference osisRef="Job.39.14">Job 39:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.10">Psa 49:10</reference>). Hell as (<reference osisRef="Gen.42.38">Ge 42:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.5">Psa 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2">Jon 2:2</reference>) the state or region of death, and so frequently--or the grave itself (<reference osisRef="Job.14.13">Job 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.17.13">17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">Ec 9:10</reference>, &c.). So the Greek Hades (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.27">Ac 2:27</reference>, 31). The context alone can settle whether the state mentioned is one of suffering and place of the damned (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.17">Psa 9:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.5">Pr 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.7.27">7:27</reference>).<div eID="gen8510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wilt ... suffer--</hi>literally, "give" or "appoint."<div eID="gen8511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Holy One--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>), one who is the object of God's favor, and so a recipient of divine grace which he exhibits--pious.<div eID="gen8512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to see--</hi>or, "experience"--undergo (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.26">Lu 2:26</reference>).<div eID="gen8513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corruption--</hi>Some render the word, the pit, which is possible, but for the obvious sense which the apostle's exposition (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.27">Ac 2:27</reference>; 13:36, 37) gives. The sense of the whole passage is clearly this: by the use of flesh and soul, the disembodied state produced by death is indicated; but, on the other hand, no more than the state of death is intended; for the last clause of <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference> is strictly parallel with the first, and Holy One corresponds to soul, and corruption to hell. As Holy One, or David (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.36">Ac 13:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.37">37</reference>), which denotes the person, including soul and body, is used for body, of which only corruption can be predicated (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.31">Ac 2:31</reference>); so, on the contrary, soul, which literally means the immaterial part, is used for the person. The language may be thus paraphrased, "In death I shall hope for resurrection; for I shall not be left under its dominion and within its bounds, or be subject to the corruption which ordinarily ensues." <div eID="gen8514" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 11. Raised from the dead, he shall die no more; death hath no more dominion over him. Thou wilt show me-- guide me to attain. the path of life-- or, "lives"--the plural denoting variety and abundance--immortal blessedness of every sort--as "life" often denotes. in thy presence-- or, "before Thy faces." In the glories of this state, He shall see of the travail ( Is 53:10 , 11 ; Php 2:9 ) of His soul, and be satisfied.

navigation_sections.title: Psa 16:1-11 . Michtam, or, by the change of one letter, Michtab--a "writing," such as a poem or song (compare Is 38:9 ). Such a change of the letter m for b was not unusual. The position of this word in connection with the author's name, being that usually occupied by some term, such as Psalm or song, denoting the style or matter of the composition, favors this view of its meaning, though we know not why this and Psalms 56-60 should be specially, called "a writing."
